prompt: A report job took 100 seconds, of which parsing was 40 seconds. A developer made parsing 4 times faster and the job now takes 70 seconds. The manager is disappointed and asks for another week to make parsing 4 times faster again. What is the best advice?

options.text: Go ahead: another 4× on parsing will bring the job down to about 25 seconds
options.explanation: That applies the speedup to the whole job. Only parsing gets faster; the other 60 seconds are untouched, so the job can never drop below 60 seconds by working on parsing.

options.text: Stop working on parsing. It is now only 10 of the 70 seconds, so even making it instant would save at most 10 seconds; profile the other 60 seconds instead
options.explanation: Correct. This is Amdahl's ceiling: the untouched 60 seconds bound what parsing work can achieve. Another 4× would save about 7.5 seconds (10 down to 2.5). The 60 seconds the team has not looked at is where the next big win, if any, has to come from.

options.text: The first change must have been done badly, because a 4× speedup should make the job 4 times faster
options.explanation: The change worked as intended: parsing fell from 40 to 10 seconds. The whole job only gets 4 times faster if parsing was the whole job.

options.text: Rewrite the whole job in a faster language, since the remaining time must be interpreter overhead
options.explanation: Nothing in the measurements says what the other 60 seconds are; they could be waiting on a database or the network. Profile before choosing a fix.

workedExample:
1. Split the original runtime: 40 s parsing, 60 s everything else.
2. After the first change, parsing takes 10 s and the job 70 s. That matches Amdahl's law: only the improved slice shrank.
3. Parsing is now a small slice (about 14% of the runtime). Even an infinitely fast parser would leave 60 s, so further parsing work can save at most 10 s; another 4× saves about 7.5 s.
4. The untouched 60 s now dominates. Profile it to find what that time is spent on (computing, or waiting on I/O), then decide whether a further target is worth pursuing at all.

prompt: Your team wants to speed up an API. A developer suggests rewriting the JSON serialisation in Rust because "JSON is always slow". What should happen first?

options.text: Do the rewrite; serialisation is a well-known bottleneck
options.explanation: It might be, but without measurement you could spend weeks speeding up something that takes 2% of each request.

options.text: Set a target (for example p99 latency) and profile real requests to find where the time actually goes
options.explanation: Correct. A target says when you are done, and a profile tells you which part is worth working on. Guesses about bottlenecks are wrong surprisingly often.
More servers can reduce queueing latency when capacity is the bottleneck, but measuring the bottleneck should precede the decision.

options.text: Turn on caching for every endpoint
options.explanation: Caching can help, but applying it everywhere without knowing the bottleneck adds staleness and complexity, possibly for no gain.

workedExample:
1. Define success: e.g. 'p99 of /orders below 250 ms'. Measure the current value.
2. Profile representative requests, including wall-clock time, not just CPU.
3. Suppose serialisation is 3% of time and a database call is 70%. By Amdahl's law, an infinitely fast serialiser saves at most 3%.
4. Work on the biggest slice, re-measure, and stop when the target is met.
